body: South Africa is located on the southern tip of Africa. It borders Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Eswatini and Lesotho.

The language of Afrikaans, which is very similar to Dutch, is almost exclusively spoken in South Africa and Namibia. It is more common in the western half of the country. English is spoken throughout the whole country. NOTE:The language is also currently rare in Botswana, but has some limited presence in the form of place names.
South Africa's most common utility poles, known as “bird poles,” feature 1 to 5 horizontal bars with thin white insulators. While other pole types exist, these are a key national identifier.
South Africa uses green directional signs with yellow road numbers. Road numbers are key for differentiation: N and R-roads are unique to South Africa.
South Africa uses triangular warning signs with a red border and white background, similar to its neighbours. This distinguishes it from the yellow diamond signs of Australia and New Zealand.
South Africa uses distinctive white-and-red chevrons. You will also find small, thin single-arrow chevrons, which are also present in neighbouring countries.
In suburban areas of large cities, houses are often protected by high walls, fences, and gates for security.
All Generation 4 coverage in South Africa was captured by a blue Street View car with a short antenna.
South Africa features Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, identifiable by its low mounting position and a large circular blur, sometimes with a small protrusion or a short rear antenna.
Each South African province has a unique license plate design. The Free State plates have a green tint, while KwaZulu-Natal plates have a blue tint, which can sometimes be seen through the blur.
Major highways are designated with an 'N' on road signs. On Google Maps, these are shown as a blue pentagon without the 'N'.
Three-digit R-roads are generally geographically grouped by their first number, providing a good clue for region-guessing. The map shows the approximate location for each road series.
South African landline area codes are geographically grouped, making them useful for location. Mobile numbers, starting with 06, 07, or 08, are not area-specific.
A-shaped pole tops, where the bottom insulators are on a horizontal bar, are a strong indicator for the Western Cape.
A wider A-shaped poletop where insulators attach directly to the 'A' frame is characteristic of the Eastern Cape.
Trident-shaped pole tops are an almost exclusive clue for KwaZulu-Natal.
Poles with 3 alternating horizontal insulators at the top are primarily found in the four northern provinces: Limpopo, Gauteng, North West, and Mpumalanga.
Poles with two diagonal bars forming a '<' shape are most common in the northeastern provinces, especially Limpopo and North West.
Poles featuring 1 or 2 metal arms holding insulators are most common in Mpumalanga.
Square red stickers on the back of regular road signs are a good indicator for the Eastern Cape and its surrounding areas. However, red stickers on chevrons are found nationwide.
White stickers on the back of chevrons are a common sight in the Cape provinces (Western, Eastern, and Northern Cape).
A grainy, pink-tinted pavement, reminiscent of Texas roads, is a distinctive feature of Limpopo province.
Large bird nests built on top of utility poles are a common clue for the northern part of the Northern Cape.
Numerous power plants are visible between Secunda and eMalahleni in Mpumalanga province.
The northeast of South Africa is often dry and barren with orange or red soil and shrub-covered hills. The landscape's appearance can vary significantly between dry and green seasons.
The Western Cape is known for its unique rocky, treeless mountains with steep sides and sharp peaks. Similar mountains are also found near Lesotho.
Vineyards are a strong indicator for the Western Cape, especially in coastal valleys. They are also found near Upington in the Northern Cape.
A dry landscape with red soil is characteristic of the Northern Cape. Refer to the climate map for more detail on regional biomes.
Sugarcane plantations are most common along the coast of KwaZulu-Natal and also appear in Mpumalanga near the Mozambique border.
Tall, distinctive Cook pine trees are a common sight along the southeastern coast, particularly between East London and Durban.
Pine tree plantations are common in South Africa to the west of Eswatini and south into KwaZulu-Natal.
Grassy rolling hills are characteristic of the Western Cape's coastal area, particularly between Cape Town and George.
Near the Mozambique border, the landscape becomes noticeably flat with green, subtropical vegetation.
A camouflage car with black mirrors and roof racks was used for the initial coverage of Kruger National Park. The park now also has Generation 4 coverage.
Kruger National Park has a flat, savannah landscape with dry grass, scattered trees, and red soil. Look for distinctive directional waystones at junctions.
Metropolitan (M) route signs have unique designs in different cities. The ones shown are specific to Port Elizabeth (Gqeberha) and Durban.
In Johannesburg, traffic light and pedestrian crossing poles have three strips of reflective tape wrapped around them.
In Durban, you can find a specific streetlight design with a distinctive bump on top of the lamp arm.
Infrastructure in the Gauteng province, especially Johannesburg, is often covered in dodgy adverts for services like abortions or penis enlargement.
The R360 north of Bokspits is a north-south road with reddish asphalt running through an arid landscape of dry trees and golden grass next to the Botswana border.
The iconic Table Mountain, west of Cape Town, is easily identified by its long, flat top, flanked by the pyramidal Devil's Peak.
From the city of George, you can see mountains to the north, which are part of the Witfontein Nature Reserve and likely include George's Peak.
